approachQuestion.prompt: A calculator receives an immutable list of n tokens, 1 <= n <= 200,000. Each token is a signed integer, ADD, or SUB. An integer contributes its value. An operator consumes the two most recent unresolved values: if the older is a and the newer is b, ADD produces a+b and SUB produces a-b. That result becomes one unresolved value. Return the final value. The list is guaranteed well formed: every operator has two values available and exactly one value remains at the end. All literals and intermediate results fit signed 64-bit integers. Choose a method minimizing worst-case total processing time. Input: [12, 5, 2, SUB, SUB]. Output: 9, since 5-2=3 and 12-3=9.

options.text: Scan left to right with a value stack. Push integers; for an operator pop b, then a, and push a+b or a-b. Return the last value.
options.feedback: Two completed subexpressions nearest the operator are its operands; preserving their order matters for subtraction.

options.text: Use a value stack, but for SUB pop b then a and push b-a.
options.feedback: For [12,5,SUB], this returns -7 instead of 7. The newest value is the right operand.

options.text: Keep values in a FIFO queue; each operator consumes the oldest two values.
options.feedback: For [12,5,2,SUB,SUB], this consumes 12 and 5 first and eventually returns -5 rather than 9.

options.text: Copy tokens to a mutable list. Repeatedly find the leftmost operator, replace its preceding two values and itself by its result, and shift the remaining suffix.
options.feedback: This correctly reduces complete subexpressions, but repeated searches and suffix shifts repeat work that a retained value stack avoids.

feedback.reason: An operator combines the latest completed values, while subtraction fixes which is left and right.
details: Keep unresolved values on a stack. An operator removes its right operand first and its left operand second, then pushes the computed value. Return the sole remaining value.

An operator pops the right operand before the left operand. This matters for subtraction and division even though addition hides the mistake. Literals remain pending until a later operator consumes them.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For reduce-operands, choose the tightest worst-case total time and auxiliary-space bounds in terms of n, the input length.
constraints: The input is immutable and excluded from auxiliary space. Returned output is excluded, but all working buffers count even if later copied into output.
Fixed-size integers, characters, indices and comparisons take constant time. Arithmetic is unit cost under the stated range guarantee.
Use an iterative implementation with a preallocated n-entry array and a top index: push and pop take constant time. No recursion, hashing, or hidden whole-buffer copies occur.
Materializing output takes time proportional to its length; no persistent snapshots or string concatenation are used.

options.text: O(log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each token causes at most two pops and one push.
details: Every token is processed once with at most two pops and one push. A legal input can begin with a linear number of literals, so the working stack needs O(n) space. The scalar output adds no working buffer.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: A legal expression may first push a linear number of literals, so the pending-value stack is not constant-sized.
“O(n²) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Each operator consumes two pending values and produces one; the algorithm never reevaluates an earlier token prefix.
“O(log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The final literal or operator can affect the result, so a complete legal expression may require all n token reads.
